title: A jealous baby (1.7)
hook: he watches an infant turn pale with jealousy and sees sin's roots
tomorrow: why would a grown man cry for a queen in a poem?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a narrow, ruined room, and a plea that God enlarge it and repair it himself. The line was come in.

There's a kind of family video: a toddler sees the new baby on mom's lap and the meltdown begins. Funny on a phone. Now the odd part. Augustine is writing a book addressed to God, about his own sins, and in the middle of it he stops to describe a baby in a nursery. Not himself; he admits he can't remember being that small. Someone else's baby. Why would a confession to God need a stranger's infant? Because he thinks something important is already happening there, before the child can say a word.
screen: `THE TODDLER AND THE NEW BABY.` → `A NURSERY, IN A CONFESSION?` → `BEFORE A SINGLE WORD.`

segments.voice: So yes: a baby who can't talk can already be jealous. Augustine says he saw it himself. One infant watches another nursing at the same breast and goes pale, staring, bitter, though there's plenty of milk for both. He adds the parts parents will recognize: the greedy crying, the fury at grownups, even its own parents, for not doing what it wants. Mothers and nurses, he says, claim to charm such tempers away with remedies of their own, and everyone puts up with it, because it passes with age. Then the line that solves the puzzle. It's the weakness of a baby's limbs that is innocent, he says, not its will. The baby is harmless because it's small, not because it wants nothing. That's why the nursery belongs in a confession. Augustine is tracing his own story back past memory and finding the same bent will there at the start. Catholic teaching calls that inheritance original sin, and counts envy among the capital sins. But listen to his tone. No horror at babies, and no blame. He's looking into a nursery and finding himself. And there's mercy in it: if envy can show up before speech, it isn't a shameful secret only you picked up. It starts early. That makes it easier to name, and worth bringing to God.
screen: `PALE, BITTER, AND PLENTY OF MILK.` · `WEAK LIMBS, NOT AN INNOCENT WILL.` · `TRACING HIMSELF PAST MEMORY.` · `NO HORROR, NO BLAME.` · then, large: `IT STARTS EARLY.`

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write the name of one small envy you've carried lately, the kind a child would recognize: someone else's praise, someone else's plate, someone else's ease. Then look at the words the way Augustine looked into the nursery, honestly and without disgust, and sit with the paper in your hand. Catholics who pray can name it to God just as plainly.
A jealous baby. In book one, Augustine watches an infant go pale with envy at another child, and sees how early the will bends.
The line to keep: it starts early, so it can be named without shame. Rest well.

Augustine.meaning: a North African bishop who wrote the Confessions as a prayer

original sin.meaning: Catholic name for the wound in human nature from the start

notes: All of 1.7 is paraphrased: he saw an envious infant who could not speak, pale and bitter at its foster-brother; greedy crying; anger at elders and parents for not serving its will; mothers and nurses' remedies; tempers borne with because they pass with age; 'the weakness of infant limbs, not its will, is its innocence'. Confirm against Pusey.
'He can't remember his own infancy' draws on 1.6–1.7 (he trusts others and observes other infants). Confirm.
'Catholic teaching calls that inheritance original sin' is descriptive; no claim is made about Augustine's influence on the doctrine. A Keeper may wish to add it or to soften 'bent'.
The index hook says 'jealousy'; the voice keeps Augustine's 'envy' and 'pale and bitter'.
